content: 1. A defaulter in treatment refers to a patient who has not adhered to the prescribed treatment regimen, either by missing doses or discontinuing treatment altogether. 2. The prevalence trend over the last five years can be assessed by compiling national and sub-national reports, reviewing leprosy registers at health centers, and engaging in discussions with national program managers. 3. The treatment completion rate should ideally be 85% or higher, as this reflects the efficiency of patient management within the program. 4. A significant challenge in data collection is obtaining accurate denominator information, such as population data at sub-national levels over the past five years. 5. Child detection trends should be analyzed by disaggregating data by age, sex, mode of detection, skin smear positivity, type of leprosy, and disability grading, if available. These parameters are optional but useful for understanding transmission trends over time. 6. Decisions regarding data collection and analysis should be made in advance, and prerequisites include compiling reports, checking leprosy registers, and consulting with program managers. 7. Detection trends must be interpreted cautiously, keeping in mind the influence of operational factors that may introduce bias. 8. Skin smears are not mandatory for diagnosis or classification, but if performed, the information should be collected for analysis. 9. Monitoring the availability of MDT (multi-drug therapy) blister packs and geographic coverage of MDT services is essential. This can be achieved through cross-sectional surveys of health facilities and patient interviews. 10. MDT services encompass comprehensive health activities, including diagnosis, classification, treatment prescription, MDT delivery, case-holding, patient cure, and counseling. 11. The proportion of health facilities providing MDT services should be assessed to evaluate accessibility. Facilities must maintain at least two months of drug stock, and definitions of health facilities should be established in consultation with relevant authorities. 12. Data collection involves obtaining lists of health facilities reporting leprosy cases, visiting selected facilities to verify MDT stock availability, and calculating the proportion of facilities with adequate MDT supplies. 13. Geographic coverage of MDT services may be influenced by factors such as national policies limiting MDT provision to specialized centers, shortages of MDT or personnel, and delays in integration processes. 14. Accessibility to MDT services should be evaluated based on geographic, financial, and technical ease of access for patients. Indicators include treatment delay, average distance traveled for MDT collection, and flexibility in MDT delivery. 15. The availability of MDT drugs should be monitored to identify potential surplus or shortage at health centers, district, and regional stores. This is expressed in terms of months of supply relative to the patient caseload. 16. The quality of MDT services, including diagnosis, case-holding, and patient information, should be reviewed through cohort analysis of individual records, leprosy registers, and community interviews. 17. Treatment outcome indicators, such as completion rate, defaulter rate, and the proportion of patients continuing treatment after completion, should be evaluated through cohort analysis of patients who started treatment during a given year. 18. The proportion of patients developing new disabilities during or after treatment should be measured to assess the quality of patient care. This involves examining clinical status and disability assessments of cases released from treatment in the last two years. 19. Patient satisfaction should be assessed through interviews and questionnaires to evaluate the quality of care from the perspective of affected individuals. This can help identify areas for improvement in service delivery. 20. Community perception of leprosy and the program should be measured to assess awareness levels and the impact of information, education, and communication (IEC) activities. This indirectly reflects the quality of services. 21. Perceived stigma among affected individuals should be evaluated to measure the prevalence of discrimination and negative attitudes within the community. This can be done through interviews and questionnaires. 22. Monitoring these indicators is crucial for evaluating the performance of leprosy programs, ensuring appropriate use of MDT, and estimating drug requirements at various levels. 23. Challenges in data collection include poor recording systems, time-consuming compilation of registers, and potential biases in patient interviews or community surveys. Careful analysis is required to ensure accurate estimates and interpretations.
